**English**—
the relation being that he by whom that Self is held most dear is most dear to the Self. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> yathāyaṁ priyatama ātmānaṁ prāpnōti,  
tathā svayam ēva bhagavān prayatata  

iti bhagavataivōktam-  

**English**—
That the Lord (bhagavān) himself endeavours that this most beloved person should gain the Self, he himself declares in the following words, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tēṣāṁ satata-yuktānāṁ  
> bhajatāṁ prītipūrvakam।  
> **dadāmi** buddhiyōgaṁ taṁ  
> yēna māmupayānti tē॥  
> (bha.gī.10.10) 

iti,  

**English**—
> 'To those who are constantly devoted and worship with love I give that knowledge by which they reach me' (Bha. Gī. X, 10), 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> priyō hi jñāninō'tyartham  
> ahaṁ sa ca mama priyaḥ॥  
> (bha.gītā.7.17) 

iti ca॥

**English**—
and 'To him who has knowledge I am dear above all things, and he is dear to me' (VII, 17). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
atas 

> sākṣāt-kāra-rūpā smr̥tiḥ  
smaryamāṇātyartha-priyatvēna  
svayam apy atyartha-priyā yasya,  
sa ēva parēṇā'tmanā varaṇīyō bhavati

iti  
tēnaiva labhyatē para ātmēty uktaṁ bhavati।

**English**—
Hence, he who possesses remembrance, marked by the character of immediate presentation (sākshātkāra), and which itself is dear above all things since the object remembered is such; he, we say, is chosen by the highest Self, and by him the highest Self is gained. 

###### dhyānam bhaktiḥ

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēvaṁ rūpā dhruvānusmr̥tir ēva  
bhaktiśabdēnābhidhīyatē,  
upāsanaparyāyatvād bhakti-śabdasya । 

**English**—
Steady remembrance of this kind is designated by the word 'devotion' (bhakti); for this term has the same meaning as upāsanā (meditation). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ata ēva śrutismr̥tibhir ēvam abhidhīyatē –

**English**—
For this reason scripture and smr̥ti agree in making the following declarations, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tam ēva viditvā 'timr̥tyum ēti (śvē.3.8) 

**English**—
> 'A man knowing him passes over death' (Śvet. Up. III, 8); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tam ēvaṁ vidvān amr̥ta iha bhavati ।  
nānyaḥ panthā ayanāya vidyatē (puruṣasūktaṁ.17)

**English**—
> 'Knowing him thus he here becomes immortal' (Taitt. Ār. III, 12,7); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nāhaṁ vēdair na tapasā  
na dānēna na cējyayā।  
śakya ēvaṁ-vidhō draṣṭuṁ  
dr̥ṣṭavān asi māṁ yathā॥ 

**English**—
> 'Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerities, nor by gifts, nor by sacrifice can I be so seen as thou hast seen me. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> bhaktyā tv ananyayā śakya  
aham ēvaṁ-vidhō'rjuna।  
jñātuṁ draṣṭuṁ ca tattvēna  
pravēṣṭuṁ ca parantapa!॥  
(bha.gī.11.53,54) 

**English**—
> But by devotion exclusive I may in this form be known and seen in truth, O Arjuna, and also be entered into' (Bha. Gī. XI, 53, 54); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> puruṣas sa paraḥ pārtha!  
bhaktyā labhyas tv ananyayā॥ 

(bha.gī.8.22) iti॥

**English**—
> 'That highest Person, O Pārtha, may be obtained by exclusive devotion' (VIII, 22).

###### karmāṅgakatvam

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēvaṁ-rūpāyā dhruvānusmr̥tēs sādhanāni  
yajñādīni karmāṇīti 

> yajñādi-śrutēr aśvavat (bra.sū.3.4.26) 

ity abhidhāsyatē । 

**English**—
That of such steady remembrance sacrifices and so on are means will be declared later on (Ve. Sū. III, 4, 26). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
yadyapi "vividaṣantī"ti yajñādayō vividaṣōtpattau viniyujyantē, 

**English**—
Although sacrifices and the like are enjoined with a view to the origination of knowledge (in accordance with the passage 'They desire to know,' Br̥. Up. IV, 4, 22), 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tathā'pi tasyaiva vēdanasya dhyāna-rūpasya  
ahar-ahar-anuṣṭhīyamānasya  
abhyāsādhēyātiśayasya  
āprayāṇād anuvartamānasya  
brahma-prāpti-sādhanatvāt  

tad-utpattayē sarvāṇy-āśrama-karmāṇi yāvaj-jīvam anuṣṭhēyāni । 

**English**—
it is only knowledge in the form of meditation which – being daily practised, constantly improved by repetition, and continued up to death – is the means of reaching Brahman, and hence all the works connected with the different conditions of life are to be performed throughout life only for the purpose of originating such knowledge. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
vakṣyati ca – 

> āprayāṇāt - tatrāpi hi dr̥ṣṭam (bra.sū.4.1.12.) 

**English**—
This the Sūtrakāra declares in Ve. Sū. IV, 1, 12; 16; III, 4, 33, and other places. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> agnihōtrādi tu tat-kāryāyaiva - tad-darśanāt (bra.s.4.1.16) 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> sahakāritvēna ca (bra.sū.3.4.33) 

ityādiṣu।

###### sādhana-saptaka-niṣpādyatvam

**vi॰pra॰**—
vākyakāraś ca dhruvānusmr̥tēr vivēkādibhya ēva niṣpattimāha –  

> tal-labghir vivēka-vimōkābhyāsa--kriyā-kalyāṇānavasādānuddharṣēbhyaḥ - sambhavān nirvacanāc ca (bra.na.vā) 

iti । 

**English**—
The Vākyakāra also declares that steady remembrance results only from abstention, and so on; his words being 

> 'This (viz. steady remembrance= meditation) is obtained through abstention (viveka), freeness of mind (vimoka), repetition (abhyāsa), works (kriyā), virtuous conduct (kalyāṇa), freedom from dejection (anavasāda), absence of exultation (anuddharsha); according to feasibility and scriptural statement.' 

###### vivēkaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
vivēkādīnāṁ svarūpaṁ cāha – 

> jāty-āśraya-nimittāduṣṭād annāt kāya-śuddhir vivēkaḥ (bra.na.vā) 

iti । 

**English**—
The Vākyakāra also gives definitions of all these terms.  

> Abstention (viveka) means keeping the body clean from all food, impure either owing to species (such as the flesh of certain animals), or abode (such as food belonging to a Cāṇḍāla or the like), or accidental cause (such as food into which a hair or the like has fallen). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
atra nirvacanam – 

> āhāra-śuddhau sattva-śuddhis  
sattva-śuddhau dhruvā smr̥tiḥ  
(chāṁ.7.26.2) 

iti । 

**English**—
The scriptural passage authorising this point is _Kh._ Up. VII, 26, 'The food being pure, the mind becomes pure; the mind being pure, there results steady remembrance.' 

###### vimōkaḥ

**vi॰pra॰**—
vimōkaḥ kāmānabhiṣvaṅgaḥ (bra.na.vā) iti। 

**English**—
Freeness of mind (vimoka) means absence of attachment to desires. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> śānta upāsīta (chā.3.14.1) 

iti nirvacanam। 

**English**—
The authoritative passage here is 'Let him meditate with a calm mind' (_Kh._ Up. III, 14, 1). 

###### abhyāsaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
> ārambhaṇa-saṁśīlanaṁ punaḥ punar abhyāsaḥ (bra.na.vā) 

iti । 

**English**—
Repetition means continued practice. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
nirvacanaṁ ca smārtam udāhr̥taṁ bhāṣyakārēṇa – 

> sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ (bha.gī.8.6) 

iti। 

**English**—
For this point the Bhāshya-kāra quotes an authoritative text from Smr̥ti, viz.: 'Having constantly been absorbed in the thought of that being' (sadā tadbhāvabhāvitaḥ; Bha. Gī.VIII, 6).

###### kriyā
**vi॰pra॰**—
> pañca-mahā-yajñādy-anuṣṭhānaṁ śaktitaḥ kriyā (bra.na.vā) । 

**English**—
--By 'works' (kriyā) is understood the performance, according to one's ability, of the five great sacrifices. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
nirvacanaṁ 

> kriyāvān ēṣa brahma-vidāṁ variṣṭhaḥ (mu.3.1.4) 

**English**—
The authoritative passages here are 'This person who performs works is the best of those who know Brahman' (Mu. Up. III, 1, 4); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tam ētaṁ vēdānuvacanēna brāhmaṇā vividiṣanti  
yajñēna dānēna tapasā 'nāśakēna (br̥.6.4.22.) 

iti ca । 

**English**—
and 

> 'Him Brāhmaṇas seek to know by recitation of the Veda, by sacrifice, by gifts, by penance, by fasting' (Br̥. Up. IV, 4, 22).

###### kalyāṇāni
**vi॰pra॰**—
> satyārjava-dayā-dānāhiṁsānabhidhyāḥ kalyāṇāni (bra.na.vā) iti । 

**English**—
--By virtuous conduct (kalyāṇāni) are meant truthfulness, honesty, kindness, liberality, gentleness, absence of covetousness. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
nirvacanaṁ 

> satyēna labhyaḥ (mu.3.1.5) 

**English**—
Confirmatory texts are 'By truth he is to be obtained' (Mu. Up. III, 1, 5) 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tēṣām ēvaiṣa virajō brahma-lōkaḥ (pra.1.15.16) 

ityādi । 

**English**—
and 'to them belongs that pure Brahman-world' (Pr. Up. I, 16).

###### anavasādaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
> dēśa-kāla-vaiguṇyāt śōka-vastv-ādy-anusmr̥tēś ca  
taj-jaṁ dainyam a-bhāsvaratvaṁ manasō 'vasādaḥ (bra.na.vā) 

iti,  

> tad-viparyayō anavasādaḥ (bra.na.vā)। 

**English**—
--That lowness of spirit or want of cheerfulness which results from unfavourable conditions of place or time and the remembrance of causes of sorrow, is denoted by the term 'dejection'; the contrary of this is 'freedom from dejection.' 

**vi॰pra॰**—
nirvacanaṁ 

> nāyam ātmā bala-hīnēna labhyaḥ (mu.u.3.4) +++(5)+++

iti । 

**English**—
The relevant scriptural passage is 'This Self cannot be obtained by one lacking in strength' (Mu. Up. III, 2, 4).

###### anuddharṣaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
> tad-viparyaya-jā tuṣṭir uddharṣaḥ (bra.na.vā) 

iti। 

> tad-viparyayō 'nuddharṣaḥ (bra.na.vā) । 

**English**—
'Exultation' is that satisfaction of mind which springs from circumstances opposite to those just mentioned; the contrary is 'absence of exultation.

**vi॰pra॰**—
atisantōṣaś ca virōdhītyarthaḥ। 

**English**—
Overgreat satisfaction also stands in the way (of meditation). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
nirvarcanamapi – śāntō dāntaḥ(br̥.6.4.23) iti।

**English**—
The scriptural passage for this is 'Calm, subdued,' &c. (Br̥. Up. IV, 4, 23).

###### āśrama-karmāpēkṣā

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēvaṁ niyama-yuktasya  
āśrama-vihita-karmānuṣṭhānēnaiva  
vidyā-niṣpattir ity uktaṁ bhavati॥ 

**English**—
--What the Vākyakāra means to say is therefore that knowledge is realised only through the performance of the duly prescribed works, on the part of a person fulfilling all the enumerated conditions.

**vi॰pra॰**—
tathā ca śrutyantaram – 

> vidyāṁ cāvidyāṁ ca  
yas tad vēdōbhayaṁ saha।  
a-vidyayā +++(karmaṇā)+++ mr̥tyuṁ tīrtvā  
vidyayā 'mr̥tam aśnutē॥  
(ī.11) 

**English**—
Analogously another scriptural passage says 'He who knows both knowledge and non-knowledge together, overcoming death by non-knowledge reaches the Immortal through knowledge' (Īs. Up. II). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
atrāvidyā-śabdābhihitaṁ varṇāśrama-vihitaṁ karma । 

**English**—
Here the term 'non-knowledge' denotes the works enjoined on the different castes and āśramas; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
avidyayā – karmaṇā, mr̥tyuṁ – jñānōtpatti-virōdhi prācīnaṁ karma, tīrtvā – apōhya, vidyayā – jñānēna, amr̥taṁ – brahma। aśnutē – prāpnōtītyarthaḥ। 

**English**—
and the meaning of the text is that, having discarded by such works death, i.e. the previous works antagonistic to the origination of knowledge, a man reaches the Immortal, i.e. Brahman, through knowledge. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
mr̥tyutaraṇōpāyatayā pratītā avidyā vidyētaradvihitaṁ karmaiva, 

**English**—
The non-knowledge of which this passage speaks as being the means of overcoming death can only mean that which is other than knowledge, viz. prescribed works. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
yathōktam – 

> iyāja sō'pi subahūn  
yajñān jñāna-vyapāśrayaḥ।  
brahma-vidyām adhiṣṭhāya  
tartuṁ mr̥tyum avidyayā॥ 
(vi.pu.6.6.12)

iti॥ 

**English**—
The word has the same sense in the following passage: 'Firm in traditional knowledge he offered many sacrifices, leaning on the knowledge of Brahman, so as to pass beyond death by non-knowledge' (Vi. Pu. VI, 6, l2).

###### pāpa-karma
**vi॰pra॰**—
jñāna-virōdhi ca karma puṇya-pāpa-rūpam । 

**English**—
--Antagonistic to knowledge (as said above) are all good and evil actions, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
brahma-jñānōtpatti-virōdhitvēnāniṣṭaphalatayā  
ubhayōr api pāpa-śabdābhidhēyatvam । +++(4)+++

**English**—
and hence – as equally giving rise to an undesirable result – they may both be designated as evil. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
asya ca jñāna-virōdhitvaṁ  
jñānōtpatti-hētu-bhūta-- śuddha-sattva-virōdhi-- rajas-tamō-vivr̥ddhi-dvārēṇa। +++(4)+++

**English**—
They stand in the way of the origination of knowledge in so far as they strengthen the elements of passion and darkness which are antagonistic to the element of goodness which is the cause of the rise of knowledge. 

###### rajas-tamasī
**vi॰pra॰**—
pāpasya ca jñānōdaya-virōdhitvam – 

> ēṣa ēvāsādhu karma kārayati  
taṁ yam adhō ninīṣati – (kau.3.6) 

iti śrutyā 'vagamyatē।

**English**—
That evil works stand in the way of such origination, the following scriptural text declares: 'He makes him whom he wishes to lead down from these worlds do an evil deed' (Ka. Up. III, 8). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
rajas-tamasōr yathā'rtha-jñānāvaraṇatvaṁ,  
sattvasya ca yathā'rtha-jñāna-hētutvaṁ bhagavataiva pratipāditaṁ –  

> sattvāt sañjāyatē jñānam (bha.gī.14.17) 

ity-ādinā । 

**English**—
That passion and darkness veil the knowledge of truth while goodness on the other hand gives rise to it, the Divine one has declared himself, in the passage 'From goodness springs knowledge' (Bha. Gī. XIV, 17). 

###### nigamanam
**vi॰pra॰**—
ataś ca jñānōtpattayē pāpaṁ karma nirasanīyam। 

**English**—
Hence, in order that knowledge may arise, evil works have to be got rid of, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tannirasanaṁ ca anabhisaṁhitaphalēnānuṣṭhitēna dharmēṇa। 

**English**—
and this is effected by the performance of acts of religious duty not aiming at some immediate result (such as the heavenly world and the like); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tathā ca śrutiḥ – 

> dharmēṇa pāpam apanudati (tai.u.6.50) 

iti।

**English**—
according to the text 'by works of religious duty he discards all evil.' 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tad ēvaṁ brahma-prāpti-sādhanaṁ jñānaṁ  
sarvāśrama-karmāpēkṣam। 

**English**—
Knowledge which is the means of reaching Brahman, thus requires the works prescribed for the different āśramas; 

###### karma-mīmāṁsāpēkṣā
**vi॰pra॰**—
atō 'pēkṣita-karma--sva-rūpa-jñānaṁ,  
kēvala-karmaṇām alpāsthira-phalatva-jñānaṁ ca  
karma-mīmāṁsā'vasēyam iti,  
saivāpēkṣitā brahma-jijñāsāyāḥ pūrvavr̥ttā vaktavyā॥

**English**—
and hence the systematic enquiry into works (i. e. the Pūrva Mīmāṁsā)--from which we ascertain the nature of the works required and also the transitoriness and limitation of the fruits of mere works – forms a necessary antecedent to the systematic enquiry into Brahman. 

###### 4-sādhanēṣu karma-mīmāṁsāpēkṣā
###### udbhavē
**vi॰pra॰**—
api ca +++(sādhana-catuṣṭayāntargata-)+++ nityānitya-vastu-vivēkādayaś ca,  
mīmāṁsā-śravaṇam antarēṇa na sampatsyantē, 

**English**—
Moreover the discrimination of permanent and non-permanent things, &c. (i.e. the tetrad of 'means' mentioned above, p. 11) cannot be accomplished without the study of the Mīmāṁsā; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
phala-karaṇa-- iti-kartavyatā -'dhikāri-viśēṣa-niścayād r̥tē,  
karma--sva-rūpa-- tat-phala-sthiratvātma-nityatvādīnāṁ duravabōdhatvāt। 

**English**—
for unless we ascertain all the distinctions of fruits of works, means, modes of procedure and qualification (on the part of the agent) we can hardly understand the true nature of works, their fruits, the transitoriness or non-transitoriness of the latter, the permanence of the Self, and similar matters. 

###### viniyōgē
**vi॰pra॰**—
ēṣāṁ sādhanatvaṁ ca viniyōgāvasēyam । 

**English**—
That those conditions (viz. nityānityavastuviveka, śama, dama, &c.) are 'means' must be determined on the basis of viniyoga ('application' which determines the relation of principal and subordinate matters – angin and anga); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
viniyōgaś ca śruti-liṅgādibhyaḥ। 

**English**—
and this viniyoga which depends on direct scriptural statement (śruti), inferential signs (linga), and so on, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
sa ca tārtīyaḥ +++(karma-mīmāṁsā-bhāgēṣu)+++। 

**English**—
is treated of in the third book of the Pūrva Mīmāṁsā-sūtras. 

###### upāsanā-karma-cintanīyatā
**vi॰pra॰**—
udgīthādy-upāsanāni karma-samr̥ddhy-arthāny api  
brahma-dr̥ṣṭi-rūpāṇi, brahmajñānāpēkṣāṇīti,  
ihaiva cintanīyāni । 

**English**—
And further we must, in this connexion, consider also the meditations on the Udgītha and similar things – which, although aiming at the success of works, are of the nature of reflections on Brahman (which is viewed in them under various forms)--and as such have reference to knowledge of Brahman. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tāny api +++(upāsanā-saṅgata-)+++karmāṇy anabhisaṁhita-phalāni brahma-vidyōtpādakānīti  
tat--sād-guṇyāpādanāny ētāni sutarām ihaiva saṅgatāni। 

**English**—
Those works also (with which these meditations are connected) aim at no special results of their own, and produce and help to perfect the knowledge of Brahman: they are therefore particularly connected with the enquiry into Brahman. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tēṣāṁ ca karma--sva-rūpādhigamāpēkṣā sarva-sammatā ॥

**English**—
And that these meditations presuppose an understanding of the nature of works is admitted by every one.

##### 6 sa-viśēṣa-mithyātvam? mahā-pūrva-pakṣaḥ

**viṣayaḥ**—
॥ iti laghusiddhāntaḥ ॥

**atha mahāpūrvapakṣaḥ॥**

**English**—
THE GREAT PŪRVAPAKSHA.  
THE ONLY REALITY IS BRAHMAN.

**viśvāsa-ṭippanī**—
mahāpūrvapakṣaṁ paṭhatē spaṣṭataram bhavati - "kathaṁ kaścana dhīmān śāṅkara-matam aṅgīkuryād" iti।  
sārahīnavādānāṁ tāvān rāśiḥ, yēna "satyaṁ syād" iti sandihyēt tādr̥śaḥ। 

###### pratijñā
**vi॰pra॰**—
yad apy āhuḥ –  

a-śēṣa--viśēṣa-pratyanīka-- cin-mātraṁ brahmaiva paramārthaḥ 

**English**—
Brahman, which is pure intelligence and opposed to all difference, constitutes the only reality; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tad-atirēki nānā-vidha--jñātr̥-jñēya--tat-kr̥ta-jñāna-bhēdādi sarvaṁ  
tasminn ēva parikalpitaṁ mithyā-bhūtaṁ –

**English**—
and everything else, i.e. the plurality of manifold knowing subjects, objects of knowledge, and acts of knowledge depending on those two, is only imagined on (or 'in') that Brahman, and is essentially false.

###### śāstrōktiḥ
###### śrutayaḥ

**vi॰pra॰**—
> sadēva sōmyēd am agra āsīd  
ēkam ēvādvitīyam (chā.6.2.1) 

**English**—
> 'In the beginning, my dear, there was that only which is, one only without a second' (Cḥ. Up. VI, 2, 1); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> atha parā yayā tad akṣaram adhigamyatē  
yat tad adrēśyam agrāhyam agōtram avarṇam  
acakṣuś-śrōtraṁ tad a-pāṇi-pādaṁ  
nityaṁ vibhuṁ sarva-gataṁ susūkṣmaṁ  
tad avyayaṁ yad  
bhūta-yōniṁ paripaśyanti dhīrāḥ ॥ (mu.1.1.6) 

**English**—
'The higher knowledge is that by which the Indestructible is apprehended' (Mu. Up. I, 1, 5); 'That which cannot be seen nor seized, which has no eyes nor ears, no hands nor feet, the permanent, the all-pervading, the most subtle, the imperishable which the wise regard as the source of all beings' (Mu. Up. I, 1, 6); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> satyaṁ jñānamanantaṁ brahma (tai.u.āna.1.1) 

**English**—
> 'The True, knowledge, the Infinite is Brahman' (Taitt. Up. II, 1); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> niṣkalaṁ niṣkriyaṁ śāntaṁ  
niravadyaṁ nirañjanam (śvē.u.6.19) 

**English**—
> 'He who is without parts, without actions, tranquil, without fault, without taint' (Śvet. Up. VI, 19); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> yasyāmataṁ tasya mataṁ  
mataṁ yasya na vēda saḥ।  
avijñātaṁ vijānatāṁ  
vijñātam avijānatām (kēna.2.3) 

**English**—
> 'By whom it is not thought, by him it is thought; he by whom it is thought knows it not. It is not known by those who know it, known by those who do not know it' (Ke. Up. II, 3); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> na dr̥ṣṭēr draṣṭāraṁ paśyēḥ  
na matēr mantāraṁ manvīthāḥ (br̥.5.4.2) 

**English**—
> 'Thou mayest not see the seer of sight; thou mayest not think the thinker of thought' (Br̥. Up. III, 4, 2); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> ānandō brahma (tai.u.bhr̥gu.6anu.) 

**English**—
> 'Bliss is Brahman' (Taitt. Up. III, 6, 1); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> idaṁ sarvaṁ yad ayam ātmā (br̥.4.4.6) 

**English**—
> 'All this is that Self' (Br̥. Up. IV, 5, 7); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nēha nānā'sti kiñcana।  
(br̥.6.4.19) 

**English**—
'There is here no diversity whatever' (Br̥. Up. IV, 4, 19); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> mr̥tyōs sa mr̥tyum āpnōti  
ya iha nānēva paśyati 

**English**—
'From death to death goes he who sees any difference here' (Ka. Up. II, 4, 10); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> yatra hi dvaitam iva bhavati  
tad itara itaraṁ paśyati  
yatra tv asya sarvamātmaivābhūt  
tat kēna kaṁ paśyēt  
tat kēna kaṁ vijānīyāt (br̥.4.4.14) 

**English**—
> 'For where there is duality as it were, there one sees the other';  
> 'but where the Self has become all of him, by what means, and whom, should he see? by what means, and whom, should he know?' (Br̥. Up. IV, 5, 15); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> vācā''rambhaṇaṁ +++(ghaṭa-śarāvādi-)+++vikārō nāma-dhēyaṁ,  
mr̥ttikēty ēva satyam (chā.6.1.4) 

**English**—
'the effect is a name merely which has its origin in speech; the truth is that (the thing made of clay) is clay merely' (Cḥ. Up. VI, 1, 4); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
yadā hy ēvaiṣa ētasminn udaram+++(→alpam??)+++ antaraṁ kurutē  
atha tasya bhayaṁ bhavati (tai.u.āna.7.2) 

**English**—
'for if he makes but the smallest distinction in it there is fear for him' (Taitt. Up. II, 7);

###### brahma-sūtrē

**vi॰pra॰**—
> na sthānatō'pi parasyōbhayaliṅgaṁ sarvatra hi (bra.sū.3.2.11) 

**English**—
--the two following Vedānta-sūtras: III, 2, 11; III, 2, 3

**vi॰pra॰**—
> māyā-mātraṁ tu kārtsnyēna -  
anabhivyakta-svarūpatvāt (bra.sū.3.2.3),

###### viṣṇu-purāṇam

**vi॰pra॰**—
> **pratyasta-mita-bhēdaṁ** yat  
sattā-mātram, agōcaram ।  
vacasām, ātma-saṁvēdyaṁ  
taj jñānaṁ **brahma-sañjñitam** ॥ 53 ॥  
(vi.pu.6.7.43) 

**English**—
--the following passages from the Vishṇu-purāṇa:

> 'In which all difference vanishes, which is pure Being, which is not the object of words, which is known by the Self only – that knowledge is called Brahman' (VI, 7, 53); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> jñāna--sva-rūpam atyanta-  
nirmalaṁ paramārthataḥ।  

> tam ēvārtha-svarūpēṇa  
bhrānti-darśanataḥ sthitam॥  
(vi.pu.1,2,6) 

**English**—
> 'Him whose essential nature is knowledge, who is stainless in reality'; 

> 'Him who, owing to erroneous view, abides in the form of things' (I, 2, 6); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> paramārthas tvam ēvaikō  
nānyō'sti jagataḥ patē!॥  
(vi.pu.1.4.38) 

**English**—
> the Reality thou art alone, there is no other, O Lord of the world!

**vi॰pra॰**—
> yad ētad dr̥śyatē mūrtam  
ētaj jñānātmanas tava। 
bhrānti-jñānēna paśyanti  
jagad-rūpam a-yōginaḥ॥ 

**English**—
> --whatever matter is seen belongs to thee whose being is knowledge; but owing to their erroneous opinion the non-devout look on it as the form of the world. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> jñāna--sva-rūpam akhilaṁ  
jagad ētad a-buddhayaḥ।  
artha-svarūpaṁ paśyantō  
bhrāmyantē mōha-samplavē॥ 

**English**—
> This whole world has knowledge for its essential nature, but the Unwise viewing it as being of the nature of material things are driven round on the ocean of delusion. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> yē tu jñāna-vidaś śuddha-  
cētasas tē 'khilaṁ jagat ।  
jñānātmakaṁ prapaśyanti  
tvad-rūpaṁ paramēśvara!॥  
(vi.pu.1.4-39,40,41) 

**English**—
> Those however who possess true knowledge and pure minds see this whole world as having knowledge for its Self, as thy form, O highest Lord!' (Vi. Pu. I, 4, 38 ff.).

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tasyātma-para-dēhēṣu  
**satō** 'py ēkamayaṁ hi yat ।  
**vijñānaṁ** paramārthō hi  
dvaitinō 'tathya-darśinaḥ॥  
(vi.pu.2.14.31) 

**English**—
> --'Of that Self, although it exists in one's own and in other bodies, the knowledge is of one kind, and that is Reality; those who maintain duality hold a false view' (II, 14, 31); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> yady anyō 'sti paraḥ kō'pi  
mattaḥ pārthiva-sattama!।  
tadaiṣō 'ham ayaṁ cānyō  
vaktum ēvam apīṣyatē॥ (vi.pu.2.13.90) 

**English**—
> 'If there is some other one, different from me, then it can be said, "I am this and that one is another"' (II, 13, 86); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> vēṇu-randhra-vibhēdēna  
bhēdaṣ ṣaḍ-jādi-sañjñitaḥ।  
abhēda-vyāpinō vāyōs  
tathā'sau paramātmanaḥ॥ +++(5)+++  
(vi.pu.2.14.32) 

**English**—
> 'As owing to the difference of the holes of the flute the air equally passing through them all is called by the names of the different notes of the musical scale; so it is with the universal Self' (II, 14, 32); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> sō'haṁ sa ca tvaṁ sa ca sarvam ētad  
ātmasvarūpaṁ **tyaja** bhēdamōham ।  
itīritas tēna sa rāja-varyas  
**tatyāja** bhēdaṁ paramārthadr̥ṣṭiḥ॥ (vi.pu.2.16.23) 

**English**—
> 'He is I; he is thou; he is all: this Universe is his form. Abandon the error of difference. The king being thus instructed, abandoned the view of difference, having gained an intuition of Reality' (II, 16, 24). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> vibhēda-janakē 'jñānē  
nāśam ātyantikaṁ gatē।  
ātmanō brahmaṇō bhēdam  
asantaṁ kaḥ kariṣyati॥  
(vi.pu.6.7.96) 

**English**—
> 'When that view which gives rise to difference is absolutely destroyed, who then will make the untrue distinction between the individual Self and Brahman?' (VI, 7, 94).

###### bhagavad-gītā
**vi॰pra॰**—
> ahamātmā guḍākēśa!  
sarva-bhūtāśaya-sthitaḥ।  
(bha.gī.10.20) 

**English**—
--The following passages from the Bhagavad-Gītā: 

> 'I am the Self dwelling within all beings' (X, 20); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> kṣētrajñaṁ cāpi māṁ viddhi  
sarvakṣētrēṣu bhārata!।  
(bha.gī.13.3) 

**English**—
> 'Know me to be the soul within all bodies' (XIII, 2); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> na tad asti vinā yat syān  
mayā bhūtaṁ carācaram॥ (bha.gī.10.93) 

**English**—
> 'Being there is none, movable or immovable, which is without me' (X, 39).

###### nigamanam
**vi॰pra॰**—
ity-ādibhir vastu--sva-rūpōpadēśa-paraiś śāstraiḥ  

> nirviśēṣacinmātraṁ brahmaiva satyam  
anyat sarvaṁ mithyā 

ity abhidhānāt।

**English**—
--All these and other texts, the purport of which clearly is instruction as to the essential nature of things, declare that Brahman only, i.e. non-differenced pure intelligence is real, while everything else is false.

###### mithyā 'vidyayā
**English**—
The appearance of plurality is due to avidyā.

###### mithyātvam
**vi॰pra॰**—
mithyātvaṁ nāma  
pratīyamānatva-pūrvaka- yathā'vasthita-vastu-jñāna-nivartyatvam,  
yathā rajjv-ādy-adhiṣṭhāna-sarpādēḥ। 

**English**—
'Falsehood' (mithyātva) belongs to what admits of being terminated by the cognition of the real thing – such cognition being preceded by conscious activity (not by mere absence of consciousness or knowledge). The snake, e.g. which has for its substrate a rope or the like is false; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
dōṣavaśād dhi tatra tat-kalpanam । 

**English**—
for it is due to an imperfection (dosha) that the snake is imagined in (or 'on') the rope. 

###### brahmaṇi
**vi॰pra॰**—
ēvaṁ cin-mātra-vapuṣi parē brahmaṇi  
dōṣa-parikalpitam idaṁ  
dēva-tiryaṅ-manuṣya--sthāvarādi-bhēdaṁ sarvaṁ jagad  
yathāvasthita-- brahma--sva-rūpāvabōdha-bādhyaṁ mithyā-rūpam ।

**English**—
In the same way this entire world, with its distinctions of gods, men, animals, inanimate matter, and so on, is, owing to an imperfection, wrongly imagined in the highest Brahman whose substance is mere intelligence, and therefore is false in so far as it may be sublated by the cognition of the nature of the real Brahman. 

###### avidyā
**vi॰pra॰**—
dōṣaś ca  
sva-rūpa--tirōdhāna-- vividha-vicitra-vikṣēpa-karī  
sad--a-sad--a-nirvacanīyā 'nādy-avidyā। 

**English**—
What constitutes that imperfection is beginningless Nescience (avidyā), which, hiding the truth of things, gives rise to manifold illusions, and cannot be defined either as something that is or as something that is not.

###### śāstrōktayaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
> anr̥tēna hi pratyūḍhāḥ (chā.8.3.2) 

**English**—
> 'By the Untrue they are hidden; ' ; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tēṣāṁ satyānāṁ satām  
a-nr̥tam apidhānam (chā.8.3.1) 

**English**—
> of them which are true the Untrue is the covering  
(Cḥ, Up. VIII, 3, 1)

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nāsad āsīn, nō sad āsīt tadānīṁ,  

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tama āsīt tamasā gūḍham agrē prakētam (yaju.2aṣṭa.8.pra.9anu.) 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> māyāṁ tu prakr̥tiṁ vidyān  
māyinaṁ tu mahēśvaram (śvē.4.10) 

**English**—
> 'Know Māya to be Prakr̥ti,  
and the great Lord him who is associated with Māya'  
(Śvet. Up. IV, 10); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> indrō māyābhiḥ puru-rūpa īyatē (br̥.4.5.19) 

**English**—
> 'Indra appears manifold through the Māyās' (Br̥. Up. II, 5, 19); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> mama māyā dur-atyayā (bha.gī.7.14) 

**English**—
> 'My Māya is hard to overcome' (Bha. Gī. VII, 14); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> an-ādi-māyayā suptō  
yadā jīvaḥ prabudhyatē (gau.2.21) 

**English**—
> 'When the soul slumbering in beginningless Māyā awakes' (Gau. Kā. I, 16).

**vi॰pra॰**—
ity-ādibhiḥ nirviśēṣa-cin-mātraṁ brahmaiva  
anādy-avidyayā sad--a-sad--anirvācyayā tirōhita-svarūpaṁ  
sva-gata-nānātvaṁ paśyatīty avagamyatē। 

**English**—
--These and similar texts teach that it is through beginningless Māyā that to Brahman which truly is pure non-differenced intelligence its own nature hides itself, and that it sees diversity within itself. 

###### purāṇāni

**vi॰pra॰**—
yathōktam –

> jñāna-svarūpō bhagavān yatō 'sāv  
a-śēṣa-mūrtir na tu vastu-bhūtaḥ।  
tatō hi śailābdhi-dharādi-bhēdān  
**jānīhi** vijñāna-vijr̥mbhitāni॥ 

**English**—
As has been said, 

> 'Because the Holy One is essentially of the nature of intelligence, the form of all, but not material; therefore know that all particular things like rocks, oceans, hills and so on, have proceeded from intelligence. 

22:1 In agreement with the use made of this passage by the Pūrvapakshin,  
vijñāna must here be understood in the sense of avidyā.  
Vijñānasabdena vividhaṁ jñāyate-neneti karaṇavyutpattyā-vidyā-bhidhiyate. Śru. Pra.

**vi॰pra॰**—
> yadā tu śuddhaṁ nija-rūpi sarva-  
karma-**kṣayē jñānam** apāsta-dōṣam।  
tadā hi saṅkalpa-tarōḥ phalāni  
**bhavanti** nō vastuṣu vastu-bhēdāḥ॥  
(vi.pu.2.12.39,40) 

**English**—
> But when, on the cessation of all work, everything is only pure intelligence in its own proper form, without any imperfections; then no differences – the fruit of the tree of wishes – any longer exist between things. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tasmān **na vijñānam r̥tē'sti** kiñcit  
kvacit kadācid dvija! vastu-jātam ।  
vijñānam ēkaṁ nija-karma-bhēda-  
vibhinna-cittair bahudhā **'bhyupētam**॥ 

**English**—
> Therefore nothing whatever, at any place or any time, exists apart from intelligence: intelligence, which is one only, is viewed as manifold by those whose minds are distracted by the effects of their own works. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> jñānaṁ viśuddhaṁ vimalaṁ viśōkam  
aśēṣa-lōbhādi-nirasta-saṅgam।  
ēkaṁ sadaikaṁ paramaḥ parēśaḥ  
sa vāsudēvō na yatō 'nyad asti॥  
(vi.pu.2.12.43,44) 

**English**—
> Intelligence pure, free from stain, free from grief, free from all contact with desire and other affections, everlastingly one is the highest Lord – Vāsudeva apart from whom nothing exists. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> sad-bhāva ēvaṁ bhavatō mayōktō  
jñānaṁ yathā satyam a-satyam anyat।  
ētat +++(vijñānaṁ)+++ tu yat saṁvyavahāra-bhūtaṁ  
tatrāpi cōktaṁ bhuvanāśritaṁ tē॥  
(vi.pu.1.12.45)

**English**—
I have thus declared to you the lasting truth of things – that intelligence only is true and everything else untrue. And that also which is the cause of ordinary worldly existence has been declared to you' (Vi. Pu. II, 12, 39, 40, 43-45).

###### avidyā-nivr̥ttiḥ

**English**—
Avidyā is put an end to by true Knowledge.

**vi॰pra॰**—
asyāś cāvidyāyā  
nirviśēṣa-cin-mātra-brahmātmaikatva-vijñānēna  
nivr̥ttiṁ vadanti – 

**English**—
Other texts declare that this Nescience comes to an end through the cognition of the essential unity of the Self with Brahman which is nothing but non-differenced intelligence. 

###### śrutayaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
> na punar mr̥tyavē,  
tad ēkaṁ paśyati, 

**English**—
> 'He does not again go to death;'   
'He sees this as one;' 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> na paśyō mr̥tyuṁ paśyati (br̥.7.26.2) 

**English**—
'He who sees this does not see death' (_Kh._ Up. VI, 27); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
yadā hy ēvaiṣa ētasminn  
adr̥śyē 'nātmyē 'niruktē 'nilayanē  
abhayaṁ pratiṣṭhāṁ vindatē।  
atha sō'bhayaṁ gatō bhavati (tai.āna.7.2) 

**English**—
> 'When he finds freedom from fear and rest in that which is invisible, incorporeal, undefined, unsupported, then he has obtained the fearless' (Taitt. Up. II, 7); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> **bhidyatē** hr̥daya-granthiś  
**chidyantē** sarva-saṁśayāḥ।  
**kṣīyantē** cāsya karmāṇi  
tasmin **dr̥ṣṭē** parāvarē (mu.2.2.8) 

**English**—
> 'The fetter of the heart is broken, all doubts are solved and all his works perish when he has been beheld who is high and low' (Mu. Up. II, 2, 8); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> brahma vēda  
brahmaiva bhavati  
(mu.3.2.9) 

**English**—
> 'He knows Brahman, he becomes Brahman only' (Mu. Up. III, 2, 9); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tam ēva viditvā 'timr̥tyum ēti  
nānyaḥ panthāḥ (śvē.3.8) 

– ity-ādyāśś rutayaḥ। 

**English**—
'Knowing him only a man passes over death; there is no other path to go' (Śvet. Up. III, 8). 

###### mr̥tyuḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
atra mr̥tyuśabdēnāvidyā'bhidhīyatē। 

**vi॰pra॰**—
yathā sanat-sujāta-vacanam – 

> pramādaṁ vai mr̥tyum ahaṁ bravīmi  
sadā 'pramādam amr̥tatvaṁ bravīmi  
(bhārata.udyōparva.41.4) 

iti।

**English**—
In these and similar passages, the term 'death' denotes Nescience;  
analogously to the use of the term in the following words of Sanatsujāta, 

> 'Delusion I call death; and freedom from delusion I call immortality' (Sanatsuj. II, 5). 

###### nirviśēṣa-brahmātmaikatva-vijñānam
###### śōdhaka-vākyāni
**vi॰pra॰**—
> satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma (tai.āna.1.anu.1) 

**English**—
'The True, knowledge, the Infinite is Brahman' (Taitt. Up. II, 1); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> vijñānam ānandaṁ brahma (br̥.5.9.28) 

**English**—
> 'Knowledge, bliss is Brahman' (Br̥. Up. III, 9, 28)--

**vi॰pra॰**—
ity-ādi--śōdhaka-vākyāvasēya- nirviśēṣa--sva-rūpa--brahmātmaikatva-vijñānaṁ ca 

**English**—
The knowledge again of the essential unity and non-difference of Brahman – which is ascertained from decisive texts such as (the above).

###### aikya-vācakāni
**vi॰pra॰**—
> atha yō'nyāṁ dēvatām upāstē-  
anyō'sāv anyō'ham asmīti  
na sa vēda (br̥.3.4.10) 

**English**—
> 'Now if a man meditates on another deity, thinking the deity is one and he another, he does not know' (Br̥. Up. I, 4, 10); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> akr̥tsnō hy ēṣaḥ (br̥.3.4.7) 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> ātmēty ēvōpāsīta (br̥.u.3.4.7) 

**English**—
> 'Let men meditate upon him as the Self (Br̥. Up. I, 4, 7); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tat tvam asi (chāṁ.u.6.8.7) 

**English**—
> 'Thou art that' (Cḥ. Up. VI, 8, 7); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tvaṁ vā aham asmi bhagavō dēvatē?  
ahaṁ vai tvam asi bhagavō dēvatē?  

**English**—
> 'Am I thou, O holy deity? and art thou me, O holy deity?'; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tad yō'haṁ sō'sau,  
yō'sau sō'ham asmi  
(ai.ā.4.2) 

**English**—
> 'What I am that is he; what he is that am I.'--

**vi॰pra॰**—
ity-ādi-vākya-siddham। 

**English**—
This is confirmed by other passages, such as (the above).

**vi॰pra॰**—
vakṣyati caitad ēva – 

> ātmēti tūpagacchanti grāhayanti ca (bra.sū.4.1.3) 

iti। 

**English**—
This the Sūtrakāra himself will declare 'But as the Self (scriptural texts) acknowledge and make us apprehend (the Lord)' (Ve. Sū. IV, 1, 3). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tathā ca vākya-kāraḥ -  

> ātmēty ēva tu gr̥hṇīyāt  
sarvasya tan-niṣpattēḥ  
(brahmanandivākyam) 

iti ।

**English**—
Thus the Vākyakāra also, 'It is the Self – thus one should apprehend (everything), for everything is effected by that.' 

**vi॰pra॰**—
anēna ca brahmātmaikatva-vijñānēna  
mithyā-rūpasya sa-+++(avidyā→)+++kāraṇasya bandhasya  
nivr̥ttir yuktā ॥

**English**—
And to hold that by such cognition of the oneness of Brahman essentially false bondage, together with its cause, comes to an end, is only reasonable.

###### pratyakṣāc chāstra-balam

**English**—
Scripture is of greater force than Perception

###### pūrva-pakṣaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
> nanu ca sakala-bhēda-nivr̥ttiḥ pratyakṣa-viruddhā katham iva śāstrajanyavijñānēna kriyatē? 

**English**—
But, an objection is raised--

> how can knowledge, springing from the sacred texts, bring about a cessation of the view of difference, in manifest opposition to the evidence of Perception?

**vi॰pra॰**—
> kathaṁ vā "rajjur ēṣā, na sarpaḥ" iti jñānēna  
pratyakṣa-viruddhā sarpa-nivr̥ttiḥ kriyatē? 

**English**—
> How then, we rejoin, can the knowledge that this thing is a rope and not a snake bring about, in opposition to actual perception, the cessation of the (idea of the) snake?

**vi॰pra॰**—
> > tatra dvayōḥ pratyakṣayōr virōdhaḥ;  
iha tu pratyakṣa-mūlasya śāstrasya  
pratyakṣasya ca
>
> iti cēt; 

**English**—
> You will perhaps reply that in this latter case there is a conflict between two forms of perception, while in the case under discussion the conflict is between direct perception and Scripture which is based on perception. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tulyayōr virōdhē vā kathaṁ bādhya-bādhaka-bhāvaḥ? 

**English**—
> But against this we would ask the question how, in the case of a conflict between two equal cognitions, we decide as to which of the two is refuted (sublated) by the other. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> > pūrvōttarayōr duṣṭa-kāraṇa-janyatva-- tad-abhāvābhyām – 
>
> iti cēt;  
śāstra-pratyakṣayōr api samānam ētat।

**English**—
> If – as is to be expected – you reply that what makes the difference between the two is that one of them is due to a defective cause while the other is not:  
we point out that this distinction holds good also in the case of Scripture and perception being in conflict. 

###### adōṣād anavakāśāt
**vi॰pra॰**—
ētad uktaṁ bhavati –  
bādhya-bādhaka-bhāvē  
tulyatva-sāpēkṣatva-nirapēkṣatvādi na kāraṇam;  
jvālā-bhēdānumānēna pratyakṣōpamardāyōgāt ।   
tatra hi jvālaikyaṁ pratyakṣēṇāvagamyatē।  

**English**—
It is not considerations as to the equality of conflicting cognitions, as to their being dependent or independent, and so on,  
that determine which of the two sublates the other;  
if that were the case, the perception which presents to us the flame of the lamp as one only would not be sublated by the cognition arrived at by inference that there is a succession of different flames. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēvaṁ ca sati  

> dvayōḥ pramāṇayōr virōdhē  
yat sambhāvyamānānyathā-siddhi, tad bādhyam;  
an-anyathā-siddham anavakāśam itarad bādhakam –  

iti sarvatra bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva-nirṇayaḥ –  

iti ॥

**English**—
> Wherever there is a conflict between cognitions based on two different means of knowledge we assign the position of the 'sublated one' to that which admits of being accounted for in some other way; while that cognition which affords no opening for being held unauthoritative and cannot be accounted for in another way, is the 'sublating one.'  
This is the principle on which the relation between 'what sublates' and 'what is sublated' is decided everywhere. 

**English - Note**—
25:1 The distinction is illustrated by the different views Perception and Inference cause us to take of the nature of the flame of the lamp. To Perception the flame, as long as it burns, seems one and the same: but on the ground of the observation that the different particles of the wick and the oil are consumed in succession, we infer that there are many distinct flames succeeding one another. And we accept the Inference as valid, and as sublating or refuting the immediate perception, because the perceived oneness of the flame admits of being accounted for 'otherwise,' viz. on the ground of the many distinct flames originating in such rapid succession that the eye mistakes them for one. The inference on the other hand does not admit of being explained in another way.

**vi॰pra॰**—
tasmāt, anādi-nidhanāvicchinna-sampradāya-- +asambhāvyamāna-dōṣa-gandhānavakāśa-  
śāstra-janya-- nirviśēṣa-nitya-- śuddha-mukta-buddha--sva-prakāśa-- cin-mātra-brahmātma-bhāvāvabōdhēna  
sambhāvyamāna-dōṣa-sāvakāśa- pratyakṣādi-siddha-- vividha-vikalpa-rūpa-- bandha-nivr̥ttir yuktaiva । 

**English**—
Now apprehension of Brahman – which is mere intelligence, eternal, pure, free, self-luminous – is effected by Scripture which rests on endless unbroken tradition, cannot therefore be suspected of any, even the least, imperfection, and hence cannot be non-authoritative;  
the state of bondage, on the other hand, with its manifold distinctions is proved by Perception, Inference, and so on,  
which are capable of imperfections and therefore may be non-authoritative. 

It is therefore reasonable to conclude that the state of bondage is put an end to by the apprehension of Brahman. 

###### anādy-avidyā-dōṣāt
**vi॰pra॰**—
sambhāvyatē ca vividha-vikalpa-bhēda-- prapañca-grāhi-pratyakṣasya  
anādi-bhēda-vāsanādi-rūpāvidyākhyō dōṣaḥ।

**English**—
And that imperfection of which Perception – through which we apprehend a world of manifold distinctions – may be assumed to be capable, is so-called Nescience, which consists in the beginningless wrong imagination of difference.

###### bhēdaśāstrān mōkṣaśāstra-balam 

**English**—
The texts which represent Brahman as devoid of qualities have greater force

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nanu anādi-nidhanāvicchinna-sampradāyatayā nirdōṣasyāpi śāstrasya  
"jyōtiṣ-ṭōmēna svarga-kāmō yajēta" ity-ēvam-ādēr bhēdāvalambinō  
bādhyatvaṁ prasajyēta। 

**English**—
> Well then-- a further objection is raised-- let us admit that Scripture is perfect because resting on an endless unbroken tradition; but must we then not admit that texts evidently presupposing the view of duality, as e.g. 'Let him who desires the heavenly world offer the Jyotishṭoma-sacrifice'--are liable to refutation?

###### paratvāt
**vi॰pra॰**—
satyam;  
+++(r̥tvik-sarpaṇē)+++ pūrvāparāpacchēdē +++(prāyaścittē karaṇīyē krama-paratva-cita-)+++ pūrva-śāstravan  
mōkṣa-śāstrasya niravakāśatvāt  
tēna bādhyata ēva । 

**English**—
--True, we reply.  
As in the case of the Udgātr̥ and Pratihartr̥ breaking the chain (not at the same time, but) in succession [fn_4], so here also the earlier texts (which refer to duality and transitory rewards) are sublated by the later texts which teach final release, and are not themselves sublated by anything else.

[fn_4]: 26:1 The reference is to the point discussed Pū. Mī. Sū. VI, 5, 54 (Jaim. Nyā. Mālā Vistara, p. 285).

**vi॰pra॰**—
vēdānta-vākyēṣv api  
sa-guṇa--brahmōpāsana-parāṇāṁ śāstraṇām  
ayam ēva nyāyaḥ,  
nirguṇatvāt parasya brahmaṇaḥ।

**English**—
The same reasoning applies to those passages in the Vedānta-texts which inculcate meditation on the qualified Brahman, since the highest Brahman is without any qualities.

###### brahma-svarūpa-saguṇatva-vākyāni

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nanu ca – "yas sarvajñas sarva-vit" (mu.u.2.2.7) 

**English**—
> But consider such passages as  
'He who cognises all, who knows all' (Mu. Up. I, 1, 9); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> > parā'sya śaktir vividhaiva śrūyatē  
svābhāvikī jñāna-bala-kriyā ca (śvē.u.6.8) 

**English**—
> > 'His high power is revealed as manifold, as essential, acting as force and knowledge' (Śvet. Up. VI, 8); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> > satya-kāmas satya-saṅkalpaḥ (chā.u.8.1.5) 

**English**—
> > 'He whose wishes are true,  
whose purposes are true' (Cḥ. Up. VIII, 1, 5); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> ity-ādi-- brahma--sva-rūpa--pratipādana-parāṇāṁ śāstrāṇāṁ kathaṁ bādhyatvam? 

**English**—
> how can these passages, which clearly aim at defining the nature of Brahman, be liable to refutation?

###### nirguṇa-vākyāni
**vi॰pra॰**—
nirguṇa-vākya-sāmarthyāt iti brūmaḥ।

**English**—
Owing to the greater weight, we reply, of those texts which set forth Brahman as devoid of qualities. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ētad uktaṁ bhavati –  

> a-sthūlam a-naṇv a-hrasvam a-dīrgham (br̥.5a.8brā.) 

**English**—
'It is not coarse, not fine, not short, not long' (Br̥. Up. III, 8, 8); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> satyaṁ jñānamanantaṁ brahma (tai.āna.1) 

**English**—
> 'The True, knowledge, infinite is Brahman' (Taitt. Up. II, 1); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nirguṇam (ātmōpaniṣat) 

**English**—
> 'That which is free from qualities,' 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nirañjanam (śvē.u.6.19.) 

**English**—
> 'that which is free from stain'

**vi॰pra॰**—
ity-ādi-vākyāni 

> nirasta-samasta-viśēṣa-- kūṭa-stha-nitya-caitanyam brahma 

\– iti pratipādayanti,  
itarāṇi ca saguṇam । 

**English**—
--these and similar texts convey the notion of Brahman being changeless, eternal intelligence devoid of all difference; while the other texts – quoted before – teach the qualified Brahman. 

###### paratvād balam
**vi॰pra॰**—
ubhaya-vidha-vākyānāṁ virōdhē  
tēnaivāpacchēdanyāyēna  
nirguṇa-vākyānāṁ +++(guṇa-bādhanē)+++ guṇāpēkṣatvēna paratvād balīyastvam  
iti na kiñcid apahīnam ॥ +++(4)+++

**English**—
And there being a conflict between the two sets of passages, we – according to the Mīmāṁsā principle referred to above – decide that the texts referring to Brahman as devoid of qualities are of greater force, because they are later in order [fn_5] than those which speak of Brahman as having qualities. Thus everything is settled.

[fn_5]: 27:1 The texts which deny all qualities of Brahman are later in order than the texts which refer to Brahman as qualified, because denial presupposes that which is to be denied.

###### satyādi-guṇāḥ?
**English**—
The text Taitt. Up. II, 1 refers to Brahman as devoid of qualities.

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nanu ca – "satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma" ityatra  
satya-jñānādayō guṇāḥ pratīyantē॥ 

**English**—
But – an objection is raised--

> even the passage 'The True, knowledge, infinite is Brahman' intimates certain qualities of Brahman, viz. true being, knowledge, infinity!--

**vi॰pra॰**—
nēty ucyatē, sāmānādhikaraṇyēnaikārthatva-pratītēḥ । 

**English**—
Not so, we reply.  
From the circumstance that all the terms of the sentence stand in co-ordination,  
it follows that they convey the idea of one matter (sense) only. 

###### aviśiṣṭam ēkam
**vi॰pra॰**—
> anēka-guṇa-viśiṣṭābhidhānē 'py ēkārthatvam a-viruddham 

\– iti cēt; an-abhidhāna-jñō dēvānāṁ priyaḥ +++(vakṣyamāṇa-rītyā)+++। 

**English**—
If against this you urge that the sentence may convey the idea of one matter only, even if directly expressing a thing distinguished by several qualities; we must remark that you display an ignorance of the meaning of language which appears to point to some weak-mindedness on your part. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēkārthatvaṁ nāma sarva-padānām arthaikyam; 

**English**—
A sentence conveys the idea of one matter (sense) only when all its constitutive words denote one and the same thing; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
viśiṣṭa-padārthābhidhānē viśēṣaṇa-bhēdēna padānām artha-bhēdō 'varjanīyaḥ; 

**English**—
if, on the othcr hand, it expresses a thing possessing several attributes, the difference of these attributes necessarily leads to a difference in meaning on the part of the individual words, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tataścaikārthatvaṁ na sidhyati। 

**English**—
and then the oneness of meaning of the sentence is lost.

###### aparyāyatvaṁ viruddhārtha-tiraskr̥tyā
**vi॰pra॰**—
> ēvaṁ tarhi sarva-padānāṁ paryāyatā syāt,  
a-viśiṣṭārthābhidhāyitvāt। 

**English**—
> But from your view of the passage it would follow that the several words are mere synonyms!

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēkārthābhidhāyitvē 'py a-paryāyatvam avahita-manāś śr̥ṇu; 

**English**—
Give us your attention, we reply,  
and learn that several words may convey one meaning  
without being idle synonyms. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēkatva-tātparya-niścayāt  
ēkasyaivārthasya tat-tat-padārtha-virōdhi-- pratyanīkatva-paratvēna  
sarva-padānām arthavattvam ēkārthatvam aparyāyatā ca॥

**English**—
From the determination of the unity of purport of the whole sentence [fn_6] we conclude that the several words, applied to one thing, aim at expressing what is opposite in nature to whatever is contrary to the meanings of the several words, and that thus they have meaning and unity of meaning and yet are not mere synonyms.

[fn_6]: 27:2 The unity of purport of the sentence is inferred from its constituent words having the same case-ending.

###### nigamanam

**vi॰pra॰**—
ētad uktaṁ bhavati -  
lakṣaṇataḥ pratipattavyaṁ brahma  
sakalētara-padārtha-virōdhi-rūpam। +++(4)+++

**English**—
The details are as follows. Brahman is to be defined as what is contrary in nature to all other things. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tad-virōdhi-rūpaṁ sarvam  
anēna pada-trayēṇa phalatō vyudasyatē। 

**English**—
Now whatever is opposed to Brahman is virtually set aside by the three words (constituting the definition of Brahman in the Taittiriya-text). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tatra satya-padaṁ vikārāspadatvēnāsatyād vastunō vyāvr̥tta-brahma-param। 

**English**—
The word 'true' (or 'truly being') has the purport of distinguishing Brahman from whatever things have no truth, as being the abodes of change; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
jñāna-padaṁ cānyādhīna-prakāśa--jaḍa-rūpād vastunō vyāvr̥tta-+++(brahma-)+++param। 

**English**—
the word 'knowledge' distinguishes Brahman from all non-sentient things whose light depends on something else (which are not self-luminous); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ananta-padaṁ ca  
dēśataḥ kālatō vastutaś ca paricchinnāt vyāvr̥tta+++(brahma-)+++param। 

**English**—
and the word 'infinite' distinguishes it from whatever is limited in time or space or nature. 

###### sarva-vyāvr̥tti-mātram
**vi॰pra॰**—
na ca vyāvr̥ttir bhāva-rūpō 'bhāva-rūpō vā dharmaḥ। 

**English**—
Nor is this 'distinction' some positive or negative attribute of Brahman, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
api tu sakalētaravirōdhi brahmaiva। 

**English**—
it rather is just Brahman itself as opposed to everything else; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
yathā śauklyādēḥ kārṣṇyādi-vyāvr̥ttis tat-padārtha--sva-rūpam ēva, na dharmāntaram +++(4)+++-  

**English**—
just as the distinction of white colour from black and other colours is just the true nature of white, not an attribute of it. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēvam ēkasyaiva vastunas  
sakalētara-virōdhy-ākāratām avagamayad  
arthavattaram ēkārtham a-paryāyaṁ ca padatrayam॥

**English**—
The three words constituting the text thus _have_ a meaning, have _one_ meaning, and are non-synonymous, in so far as they convey the essential distinction of one thing, viz. Brahman from everything else. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tasmād 

> ēkam ēva brahma svayaṁ-jyōtir  
nirdhūta-nikhila-viśēṣam 

ity uktaṁ bhavati । 

**English**—
The text thus declares the one Brahman which is self-luminous and free from all difference. 

###### kāraṇa-vākyēṣv api

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēvaṁ vākyārtha-pratipādanē saty ēva 

> sad ēva sōmyēdam agra āsīd  
ēkam ēvādvitīyam (chāṁ.6.2.1) – 

ity-ādibhir aikārthyam।

**English**—
On this interpretation of the text we discern its oneness in purport with other texts, such as 

> 'Being only this was in the beginning, one only, without a second.' 

###### svarūpaṁ samānam
**vi॰pra॰**—
> yatō vā imāni bhūtāni jāyantē (tai.bhr̥gu.1.anu.) 

**English**—
> 'That from whence these beings are born' (Taitt. Up. III, 1); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
sad ēva sōmyēdam agra āsīt (chāṁ.6.2.1) 

**English**—
> 'Being only this was in the beginning' (Cḥ. Up. VI, 2, 1); 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> ātmā vā idam ēka ēvāgra āsīt (ai.1.1.1) 

**English**—
> 'Self alone was this in the beginning' (Br̥. Up. I, 4, 1), &c., 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ity-ādibhir jagat-kāraṇatayōpalakṣitasya brahmaṇaḥ sva-rūpam idam ucyatē –  

> satyaṁ jñānamanantaṁ brahma (tai.āna.1.1) 

iti। 

**English**—
Texts such as (the above) describe Brahman as the cause of the world; and of this Brahman the Taittirīya passage 'The True, knowledge, infinite is Brahman' gives the strict definition.

**vi॰pra॰**—
tatra sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāyēna  
kāraṇa-vākyēṣu sarvēṣu  
sa-jātīya--vijātīya-vyāvr̥ttam  
advatīyaṁ brahmāvagatam। 

**English**—
In agreement with the principle that all śākhās teach the same doctrine we have to understand that, in all the texts which speak of Brahman as cause, Brahman must be taken as being 'without a second', i.e. without any other being of the same or a different kind; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
jagat-kāraṇatayōpalakṣitasya brahmaṇō 'dvitīyasya  
pratipipādayiṣitaṁ svarūpaṁ  
+++("satyaṁ jñānam anantam"→)+++ tad-avirōdhēna vaktavyam। 

**English**—
and the text which aims at defining Brahman has then to be interpreted in accordance with this characteristic of Brahman, viz. its being without a second. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
a-dvitīyatva-śrutir  
guṇatō'pi sa-dvitīyatāṁ na sahatē। 

**English**—
The statement of the Cḥāndogya as to Brahman being without a second must also be taken to imply that Brahman is non-dual as far as qualities are concerned;  

**vi॰pra॰**—
anyathā "nirañjanam" (śvē.6.19) "nirguṇam" (ātmōpaniṣat) ity-ādibhiś ca virōdhaḥ। 

**English**—
otherwise it would conflict with those passages which speak of Brahman as being without qualities and without stain. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ataś caital-+++(jagat-kāraṇatva-)+++lakṣaṇa-vākyam  
a-khaṇḍaika-rasam ēva pratipādayati।

**English**—
We therefore conclude that the defining Taittirīya-text teaches Brahman to be an absolutely homogeneous substance.

###### lakṣaṇaucitam

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nanu ca satya-jñānādi-padānāṁ svārtha-prahāṇēna  
svārtha-virōdhi-- vyāvr̥tta-vastu-svarūpōpasthāpana-paratvē  
lakṣaṇā syāt। +++(4)+++

**English**—
> But, the above explanation of the passage being accepted, it follows that the words 'true being,' 'knowledge,' &c., have to be viewed as abandoning their direct sense, and merely suggesting a thing distinct in nature from all that is opposite (to what the three words directly denote), and this means that we resort to so-called implication (implied meaning, lakshaṇā)!--

**vi॰pra॰**—
naiṣa dōṣaḥ,  
abhidhāna-vr̥ttēr api  
tātparya-vr̥ttēr balīyastvāt। 

**English**—
What objection is there to such a proceeding? we reply. The force of the general purport of a sentence is greater than that of the direct denotative power of the simple terms, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
sāmānādhikaraṇyasya hy  
aikya ēva tātparyam  
iti sarva-sammatam।

**English**—
and it is generally admitted that the purport of grammatical co-ordination is oneness (of the matter denoted by the terms co-ordinated).

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nanu ca – vākyē sarva-padānāṁ lakṣaṇā na dr̥ṣṭacarī। 

**English**—
> But we never observe that all words of a sentence are to be understood in an implied sense!--

**vi॰pra॰**—
tataḥ kim? vākya-tātparyāvirōdhē saty  
ēkasyāpi na dr̥ṣṭā +++(lakṣaṇā)+++। 

**English**—
Is it then not observed, we reply, that (not even) _one_ word is to be taken in its implied meaning if ~~otherwise~~ it would('nt) contradict the purport of the whole sentence?

**vi॰pra॰**—
samabhivyāhr̥ta-pada-samudāyasya  
ētat tātparyam iti niścitē sati  
dvayōs trayāṇāṁ sarvēṣāṁ vā tad-avirōdhāya  
ēkasyēva lakṣaṇā na dōṣāya। +++(5)+++

**viśvāsa-ṭippanī**—
anēna granthapīḍanēnēṣṭābhiprāyōdbhāvanaṁ sammatam :-D।

**English**—
And if the purport of the sentence, which is nothing but an aggregate of words employed together, has once been ascertained, why should we not take two or three or all words in an implied sense – just as we had taken one – and thus make them fit in with the general purport? 

###### prābhākara-sammatiḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
tathā ca śāstra-sthair abhyupagamyatē ॥

**English**—
(This is) in agreement herewith those scholars 

**vi॰pra॰**—
kārya-vākyārtha-vādibhiḥ  
laukika-vākyēṣu sarvēṣāṁ padānāṁ lakṣaṇā samāśrīyatē। 

**English**—
who explain to us the sense of imperative sentences, teach that in imperative sentences belonging to ordinary speech all words have an implied meaning only (not their directly denotative meaning). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
a-pūrva-kārya ēva liṅ-ādēr mukhya-vr̥ttatvāt  
liṅ-ādibhiḥ +++(laukika-)+++kriyā-kāryaṁ lakṣaṇayā pratipādyatē। +++(4)+++

**English**—
For, they maintain, imperative forms have their primary meaning only in (Vedic) sentences which enjoin something not established by other means; and hence in ordinary speech the effect of the action is conveyed by implication only. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> kāryānvita-svārthābhidhāyināṁ cētarēṣāṁ padānām  
a-pūrva--kāryānvita ēva mukhyārtha  

iti +++(laukika-)+++kriyā-kāryānvita-pratipādanaṁ  
lākṣaṇikam ēva । 

**English**—
The other words also, which form part of those imperative sentences and denote matters connected with the action, have their primary meaning only if connected with an action not established by other means; while if connected with an ordinary action they have a secondary, implied, meaning only [fn_7].

**English - Note**—
[fn_7]: 30:1 The theory here referred to is held by some of the Mīmāṁsakas. 

The imperative forms of the verb have their primary meaning, i.e. the power of originating action, only in Vedic sentences which enjoin the performance of certain actions  
for the bringing about of certain ends:  
no other means of knowledge but the Veda  
informing us that such ends can be accomplished by such actions.  
Nobody, e.g. would offer a soma sacrifice in order to obtain the heavenly world,  
were he not told by the Veda to do so. 

In ordinary life, on the other hand, no imperative possesses this entirely unique originative force,  
since any action which may be performed in consequence of a command may be prompted by other motives as well:  
it is, in technical Indian language, established already, apart from the command, by other means of knowledge.  

The man who, e.g. is told to milk a cow might have proceeded to do so, apart from the command, for reasons of his own.  
Imperatives in ordinary speech are therefore held not to have their primary meaning,  
and this conclusion is extended, somewhat unwarrantably one should say, to all the words entering into an imperative clause.

###### nigamanam
**vi॰pra॰**—
atō vākya-tātparyāvirōdhāya  
sarva-padānāṁ lakṣaṇā'pi na dōṣaḥ। 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ata idam ēvārtha-jātaṁ pratipādayantō vēdāntāḥ pramāṇam॥

###### nirviśēṣa-pratyakṣam

**English**—
Perception reveals to us non-differenced substance only

**vi॰pra॰**—
pratyakṣādi-virōdhē ca  
śāstrasya balīyastvam uktam। 

**English**—
We have so far shown that in the case of a conflict between Scripture and Perception and the other instruments of knowledge, Scripture is of greater force. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
sati ca virōdhē  
balīyastvaṁ vaktavyam। 

**vi॰pra॰**—
virōdha ēva na dr̥śyatē,  
nirviśēṣa--san-mātra-- brahma-grāhitvāt pratyakṣasya।

**English**—
The fact, however, is that no such conflict is observed to exist,  
since Perception itself gives rise to the apprehension of a non-differenced Brahman whose nature is pure Being.

###### ēka-vyavahāra-hētutā
**vi॰pra॰**—
> nanu ca – "ghaṭō'sti, paṭō'sti"  
iti nānākāra-vastu-viṣayaṁ pratyakṣaṁ  
katham iva san-mātra-grāhīty ucyatē?

**English**—
> But how can it be said that Perception, which has for its object things of various kinds – and accordingly expresses itself in judgments such as 'Here is a jar,' 'There is a piece of cloth'--causes the apprehension of mere Being? 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> vilakṣaṇa-grahaṇābhāvē sati  
sarvēṣāṁ jñānānām ēka-viṣayatvēna  
dhārā-vāhika-vijñānavad ēka-vyavahāra-hētutaiva syāt। 

**English**—
If there were no apprehension of difference, all cognitions would have one and the same object, and therefore would give rise to one judgment only – as takes place when one unbroken perceptional cognition is continued for some time.

**vi॰pra॰**—
satyam; tathaivātra vivicyatē। 

**English**—
--True. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
kathaṁ?

**vi॰pra॰**—
"ghaṭō'stī"ty-atrāstitvaṁ tad-bhēdaśca vyavahriyatē;  

**English**—
We therefore have to enquire in what way,in the judgment 'here is a jar,' an assertion is made about being as well as some special form of being. 

###### pratyakṣa-mūlaṁ svarūpam
**vi॰pra॰**—
na ca dvayōr api vyavahārayōḥ pratyakṣa-mūlatvaṁ sambhavati,  
tayōr bhinna-kāla-jñāna-phalatvāt,  
pratyakṣa-jñānasya caika-kṣaṇa-vartitvāt। 

**viśvāsa-ṭippanī**—
> ēka-kṣaṇa-vartitvē'pi  
pratyakṣa-jñānasya tasminn ēva kṣaṇē vastu-bhēda-rūpa-- tat-saṁsthāna-rūpa-gōtvādēr gr̥hītatvāt  
kṣaṇāntara-grāhyaṁ na kiñcid iha tiṣṭhati॥

iti prativakṣyati। 

**English**—
These implied judgments cannot both be founded on perception, for they are the results of acts of cognition occupying different moments of time, while the perceptional cognition takes place in one moment (is instantaneous). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tatra svarūpaṁ vā bhēdō vā pratyakṣasya viṣaya  
iti vivēcanīyam। 

**English**—
We therefore must decide whether it is the essential nature of the jar, or its difference from other things, that is the object of perception. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
bhēda-grahaṇasya  
sva-rūpa--grahaṇa-- tat-pratiyōgi--  
smaraṇa-savyapēkṣatvād ēva  
svarūpa-viṣayatvam avaśyāśrayaṇīyam iti  
na bhēdaḥ pratyakṣēṇa gr̥hyatē। 

**English**—
And we must adopt the former alternative,  
because the apprehension of difference presupposes the apprehension of the essential nature of the thing,  
and, in addition, the remembrance of its counterentities (i.e. the things from which the given thing differs).  

###### bhēda-bhrāntiḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
atō bhrānti-mūla ēva bhēda-vyavahāraḥ॥

**English**—
Hence difference is not apprehended by Perception; and all judgments and propositions relative to difference are founded on error only.

###### bhēdō na pratyakṣam
**vi॰pra॰**—
kiñca bhēdō nāma kaścit padārthō  
nyāya-vidbhir nirūpayituṁ na śakyatē। 

**English**—
Difference – bheda – does not admit of logical definition

###### na svarūpam
###### bhēda-vyavahāraḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
bhēdas tāvan na vastu-svarūpam,  
vastu-svarūpē gr̥hītē  
sva-rūpa--vyavahāravat sarvasmād-bhēda-vyavahāra-prasaktēḥ। 

**English**—
The Logicians, moreover, are unable to give a definition of such a thing as 'difference.' Difference cannot in the first place be the essential nature (of that which differs); for from that it would follow that on the apprehension of the essential nature of a thing there would at once arise not only the judgment as to that essential nature but also judgments as to its difference from everything else.

###### pratiyōgi-smaraṇānapēkṣā
**vi॰pra॰**—
na ca vācyaṁ – 

> svarūpē gr̥hītē'pi  
"bhinna" iti vyavahārasya pratiyōgi-smaraṇa-sa-vyapēkṣatvāt,  
tat-smaraṇābhāvēna tadānīm ēva na bhēda-vyavahāraḥ 

\– iti - 

**English**—
--But, it may be objected to this, 

> even when the essential nature of a thing is apprehended, the judgment 'this thing is different from other things' depends on the remembrance of its counterentities, and as long as this remembrance does not take place so long the judgment of difference is not formed!--

Such reasoning, we reply, is inadmissible.  

**vi॰pra॰**—
sva-rūpa--mātra-bhēda-vādinō hi  
pratiyōgy-apēkṣā ca nōtprēkṣituṁ kṣamā,  
sva-rūpa--bhēdayōs sva-rūpatvāviśēṣāt +++(vakṣyamāṇa-rītyā)+++। 

**English**—
He who maintains that 'difference' is nothing but 'essential nature'  
has no right to assume a dependence on counterentities  
since, according to him, essential nature and difference are the same, i.e. nothing but essential nature:  

**vi॰pra॰**—
yathā sva-rūpa-vyavahārō na pratiyōgy-apēkṣaḥ,  
bhēda-vyavahārō'pi tathaiva syāt। 

**English**—
the judgment of difference can, on his view, depend on counterentities no more than the judgment of essential nature does. 

###### bhēda-paryāyatā
**vi॰pra॰**—
"hastaḥ, karaḥ" itivat  
"ghaṭō, bhinna" iti paryāyatvaṁ ca syāt। 

**English**—
His view really implies that the two words 'the jar' and 'different' (in the judgment 'the jar is different') are synonymous, just as the words 'hasta' and 'kara' are (both of which mean 'hand').

###### na dharmaḥ

**vi॰pra॰**—
nāpi dharmaḥ; 

**English**—
Nor, in the second place, can 'difference' be held to be an attribute (dharma). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
dharmatvē sati  
tasya sva-rūpād bhēdō 'vaśyāśrayaṇīyaḥ,  
anyathā sva-rūpam ēva syāt। 

**English**—
For if it were that, we should have to assume that 'difference' possesses difference (i.e. is different) from essential nature; for otherwise it would be the same as the latter. 

###### anavasthā
**vi॰pra॰**—
bhēdē ca tasyāpi bhēdas tad-dharmas, tasyāpīty anavasthā। 

**viśvāsa-ṭippanī**—
> saṁvēdanavad rūpādivac ca  
paratra +++(viṣayē viśēṣyē ca)+++ vyavahāra-viśēṣa-hētōs  
svasminn +++(→saṁvēdana-rūpādāv)+++ api tad-vyavahāra-hētutvaṁ  
yuṣmābhir abhyupētaṁ  
bhēdasyāpi sambhavaty ēva।

iti prati-vakṣyatē। 

**English**—
And this latter difference would have to be viewed as an attribute of the first difference, and this would lead us on to a third difference, and so in infinitum. 

###### anyō'nyāśrayaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
kiñca jāty-ādi-viśaṣṭa-vastu-grahaṇē sati bhēda-grahaṇam,  
bhēda-grahaṇē sati jāty-ādi-viśiṣṭa-vastu-grahaṇam ity anyō'nyāśrayaṇam। 

**viśvāsa-ṭippanī**—
jāty-ādivad bhēdō'pi viśēṣō nāstīti katham?  
vakṣyati - 

> saṁsthānam ēva jātiḥ। … gōtvādirēva bhēdaḥ।

**English**—
And the view of 'difference' being an attribute would further imply that difference is apprehended on the apprehension of a thing distinguished by attributes such as generic character and so on, and at the same time that the thing thus distinguished is apprehended on the apprehension of difference; and this would constitute a logical seesaw.

###### nigamanam
**vi॰pra॰**—
atō bhēdasya durnirūpatvāt  
san-mātrasyaiva prakāśakaṁ pratyakṣam॥

**English**—
'Difference' thus showing itself incapable of logical definition, we are confirmed in our view that perception reveals mere 'Being' only.

###### anuvartamāna-vyāvartamāna-bhēdaḥ
###### sattāmātrānubhūtir anuvartamānā

**vi॰pra॰**—
kiñca 

> ghaṭō'sti  
paṭō'sti  
ghaṭō'nubhūyatē  
paṭō'nubhūyatē 

iti sarvē padārthās  
sattānubhūti-ghaṭitā ēva dr̥śyantē। 

**English**—
Moreover, it appears that in states of consciousness such as 'Here is a jar,' 'There is a piece of cloth,' 'The jar is perceived,' 'The piece of cloth is perceived,' that which constitutes the things is Being (existence; sattā) and perception (or 'consciousness'; anubhūti). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
atra sarvāsu pratipattiṣu  
san-mātram anuvartamānaṁ dr̥śyata  
iti tadēva paramārthaḥ।

**English**—
And we observe that it is pure Being only which persists in all states of cognition: this pure Being alone, therefore, is _real_. 

###### viśēṣā vyāvartamānāḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
viśēṣās tu vyāvartamānatayā 'paramārthāḥ,  
rajju-sarpādivat। 

**viśvāsa-ṭippanī**—
> bādhitasyaiva vyāvr̥ttiḥ।  
atra ghaṭa-paṭādiṣu dēśa-kāla-bhēdēna virōdha ēva nāsti। 

iti rajju-sarpādiṣv iva vyāvr̥tti-śabdasyārthāntaraṁ varaṁ prativakṣyati।

**English**—
The differences, on the other hand, which do not persist, are unreal. The case is analogous to that of the snake-rope. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
yathā rajjur adhiṣṭhānatayā 'nuvartamānā  
paramārthā satī;  
vyāvartamānās sarpa-bhū-dalanāmbu-dhārādayō 'paramārthāḥ।

**English**—
The rope which persists as a substrate is real, while the non-continuous things (which by wrong imagination are superimposed on the rope) such as a snake, a cleft in the ground, a watercourse, and so on, are unreal.

###### bādhāyāṁ vyāvr̥ttiḥ
###### bādhā-mātrē?
**vi॰pra॰**—
> nanu ca rajju-sarpādau  
"rajjur iyaṁ na sarpaḥ" ityādi rajjv-ādy-adhiṣṭhāna-yāthārthya-jñānēna bādhitatvāt  
sarpādēr apāramārthyam,  
na vyāvartamānatvāt। 

**English**—
But – our adversary objects--

> the instance is not truly analogous. In the case of the snake-rope the non-reality of the snake results from the snake's being sublated (bādhita) by the cognition of the true nature of the substrate 'This is a rope, not a snake'; it does not result from the non-continuousness of the snake. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> rajjv-ādēr api pāramārthyaṁ nānuvartamānatayā,  
kiṁ tv a-bādhitatvāt। 

**English**—
In the same way the reality of the rope does not follow from its persistence, but from the fact of its being not sublated (by another cognition). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> atra tu ghaṭādīnām abādhitānāṁ katham apāramārthyam?

**English**—
> But what, we ask, establishes the non-reality of jars and pieces of cloth?--

###### bādha-phalaṁ viṣaya-nivr̥ttiḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
ucyatē,  
ghaṭādau dr̥ṣṭā vyāvr̥ttis  
sā kiṁ-rūpēti vivēcanīyam। 

**English**—
All are agreed, we reply, that we observe, in jars and similar things, individual difference (vyāvr̥tti, literally 'separation,' 'distinction').  
The point to decide is of what nature such difference is. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
kiṁ ghaṭō'stīty-atra paṭādy-a-bhāvaḥ? 

**English**—
Does it not mean that the judgment 'This is a jar' implies the negation of pieces of cloth and other things? 

**vi॰pra॰**—
siddhaṁ tarhi ghaṭō'stīty-anēna paṭādīnāṁ bādhitatvam। 

**English**—
But this means that by this judgment pieces of cloth and other things are sublated (bādhita). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
atō bādha-phala-bhūtā viṣaya-nivr̥ttir vyāvr̥ttiḥ। 

**English**—
Individual difference (vyāvr̥tti) thus means the cessation (or absence), due to sublation, of certain objects of cognition, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
sā vyāvartamānānām a-pāramārthyaṁ sādhayati। 

**viśvāsa-ṭippanī**—
> dēśa-kālāntara-vyāvartamānatvaṁ  
(dēśa-kālāntara-dr̥ṣṭasya dēśāntara-kālāntara-vyāvartamānatvaṁ) –  
mithyātva-vyāptaṁ na dr̥ṣṭam iti  
na vyāvartamānatva-mātram a-pāramārthya-hētuḥ॥+++(5)+++

iti prativakṣyati। 

**English**—
and it proves the non-reality of whatever has non-continuous existence; 

###### nigamanam
**vi॰pra॰**—
rajjuvat san-mātram abādhitam anuvartatē। 

**English**—
while on the other hand, pure Being, like the rope, persists non-sublated. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tasmāt san-mātrātirēki sarvam a-paramārthaḥ। 

**English**—
Hence everything that is additional to pure Being is non-real.

**vi॰pra॰**—
prayōgaś ca bhavati –  
sat paramārthaḥ, anuvartamānatvāt, rajju-sarpādau rajjv-ādivat। 

**English**—
--This admits of being expressed in technical form. 'Being' is real because it persists, as proved by the case of the rope in the snake-rope; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ghaṭādayō 'paramārthāḥ,  
vyāvartamānatvāt,  
rajjv-ady-adhiṣṭhāna-sarpādivat – iti।

**English**—
jars and similar things are non-real because they are non-continuous, as proved by the case of the snake that has the rope for its substrate.

###### anubhūtiḥ
###### sat-anubhūtyōr aikyam

**English**—
Being and consciousness are one. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēvaṁ saty anuvartamānā 'nubhūtir ēva paramārthaḥ;  
saiva satī॥

**English**—
From all this it follows that persisting consciousness only has real being; it alone is.

**vi॰pra॰**—
> nanu ca san-mātram  
anubhūtēr viṣayatayā  
tatō bhinnam। 

**English**—
But, our adversary objects, 

> as mere Being is the object of consciousness, it is different therefrom (and thus there exists after all 'difference' or 'plurality').--

**vi॰pra॰**—
naivam;  
bhēdō hi pratyakṣāviṣayatvād durnirūpatvāc ca  
purastād ēva nirastaḥ। 

**English**—
Not so, we reply. That there is no such thing as 'difference,' we have already shown above on the grounds that it is not the object of perception, and moreover incapable of definition. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ata ēva satō 'nubhūti-viṣaya-bhāvō'pi  
na pramāṇa-padavīm anusarati। 

**English**—
It cannot therefore be proved that 'Being' is the object of consciousness. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tasmāt, sat anubhūtir ēva।

**English**—
Hence Consciousness itself is 'Being'--that which is.

###### svayam-prakāśatā
**English**—
Consciousness is svayaṁprakāsa.

**vi॰pra॰**—
sā ca svatas siddhā,  
anubhūtitvāt। 

**English**—
--This consciousness is self-proved, just because it is consciousness. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
anyatas siddhau  
ghaṭādivad ananubhūtitva-prasaṅgaḥ।

**English**—
Were it proved through something else, it would follow that like jars and similar things it is not consciousness. 

###### anubhūtyantarānapēkṣā

**vi॰pra॰**—
kiñca anubhavāpēkṣā cānubhūtēr na śakyā kalpayituṁ,  
sattayaiva prakāśamānatvāt। 

**English**—
Nor can there be assumed, for consciousness, the need of another act of consciousness (through which its knowledge would be established); for it shines forth (prakāśate) through its own being. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
na hy anubhūtir vartamānā  
ghaṭādivad aprakāśā dr̥śyatē,  
yēna parāyatta-prakāśā 'bhyupagamyēta॥

**English**—
While it exists, consciousness – differing therein from jars and the like – is never observed not to shine forth, and it cannot therefore be held to depend, in its shining forth, on something else.

###### viṣayē saty api
###### anubhūtēr anumēyatā?
**vi॰pra॰**—
athaivaṁ manuṣē – 

> utpannāyām apy anubhūtau  
viṣaya-mātram avabhāsatē  
"ghaṭō'nubhūyatē" iti। 

**English**—
You (who object to the above reasoning) perhaps hold the following view:--

> even when consciousness has arisen,  
it is the object only which shines forth--  
a fact expressed in sentences such as:  
"the jar is perceived". 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> na hi kaścid "ghaṭō'yam" iti jānan  
tadānīm ēvāviṣaya-bhūtām an-idam-bhāvām-anubhūtim apy anubhavati। 

**English**—
> When a person forms the judgment 'This is a jar,' he is not at the time conscious of a consciousness which is not an object and is not of a definite character. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> tasmād ghaṭādi-prakāśa-niṣpattau  
cakṣur-ādi-karaṇa-sannikarṣavad anubhūtēs sadbhāva ēva hētuḥ। 

**English**—
> Hence the existence of consciousness is the reason which brings about the 'shining forth' of jars and other objects, and thus has a similar office as the approximation of the object to the eye or the other organs of sense (which is another condition of perceptive consciousness). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tad-anantaram artha-gata-kādācitka-- prakāśātiśaya-liṅgēnānubhūtir anumīyatē।

**English**—
After this the existence of consciousness is inferred on the ground that the shining forth of the object is (not permanent, but) occasional only [fn_8]. 

[fn_8]: 34:1 Being not permanent but occasional, it is an effect only, and as such must have a cause.

###### jaḍatā?
**vi॰pra॰**—
> > ēvaṁ tarhy anubhūtēr a-jaḍāyā  
arthavaj jaḍatvam āpadyata 
> 
> iti cēt; 

**English**—
> And should this argumentation be objected to on the ground of its implying that consciousness – which is essentially of the nature of intelligence – is something non-intelligent like material things, 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> kim idam a-jaḍatvaṁ nāma?  
na tāvat sva-sattāyāḥ prakāśāvyabhicāraḥ,  
sukhādiṣv api tat-sambhavāt;  
na hi kadācidapi sukhādayas santō nōpalabhyantē; 

**English**—
> we ask you to define this negation of non-intelligence (which you declare to be characteristic of consciousness). Have we, perhaps, to understand by it the invariable concomitance of existence and shining forth? If so, we point out that this invariable concomitance is also found in the case of pleasure and similar affections;  
for when pleasure and so on exist at all, they never are non-perceived (i.e. they exist in so far only as we are conscious of them). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
> atō'nubhūtis svayam ēva nānubhūyatē,  
arthāntaraṁ spr̥śatō 'ṅguly-agrasya  
svātma-sparśavad a-śakyatvād 

iti॥

**English**—
> It is thus clear that we have no consciousness of consciousness itself – just as the tip of a finger, although touching other things, is incapable of touching itself.

###### nānumēyatā
**vi॰pra॰**—
tad idam anākilatānubhava-vibhavasya sva-mati-vijr̥mbhitam, 

**English**—
All this reasoning, we reply, is entirely spun out of your own fancy, without any due consideration of the power of consciousness. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
anubhūti-vyatirēkiṇō  
viṣaya-dharmasya prakāśasya  
rūpādivad anupalabdhēḥ; 

**English**—
The fact is, that in perceiving colour and other qualities of things, we are not aware of a 'shining forth' as an attribute of those things, and as something different from consciousness; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ubhayābhyupētānubhūtyaiva  
aśēṣa-vyavahārōpapattau  
prakāśākhya-dharma-kalpanānupapattēś ca। 

**English**—
nor can the assumption of an attribute of things called 'light,' or 'shining forth,' be proved in any way, since the entire empirical world itself can be proved only through consciousness, the existence of which we both admit. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
atō nānubhūtir anumīyatē। nāpi jñānāntara-siddhā। 

**English**—
Consciousness, therefore, is not something which is inferred or proved through some other act of knowledge; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
api tu sarvaṁ sādhayanty anubhūtis  
svayam ēva siddhyati। 

**English**—
but while proving everything else it is proved by itself. 

###### anumāna-prayōgaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
prayōgaś ca –  
anubhūtir an-anyādhīna--sva-dharma--vyavahārā  
sva-sambandhād arthāntarē tad+++(→arthāntara-)+++-dharma-vyavahāra-hētutvāt +++(rūpādivat, vakṣyamāṇa-rītyā)+++। 

**English**—
This may be expressed in technical form as follows--  
Consciousness is, with regard to its attributes and to the empirical judgments concerning it, independent of any other thing, because through its connexion with other things it is the cause of their attributes and the empirical judgments concerning them. 

###### rūpavat
**vi॰pra॰**—
yas +++(→dharmaḥ)+++ sva-sambandhād  
arthāntarē +++(→dharmiṇi)+++ yad-dharma-vyavahāra-hētus  
sa +++(dharmaḥ)+++ tayōs svasminn +++(vyavahārāya)+++ an-anyādhīnō dr̥ṣṭaḥ;  
yathā rūpādiś cākṣuṣatvādau। 

**English**—
For it is a general principle that  
of two things  
that which through its connexion with the other is the cause of the attributes of – and the empirical judgments about – the latter,  
is itself independent of that other as to those two points.  

**vi॰pra॰**—
rūpādir hi  
pr̥thivy-ādau svasambandhāc cākṣuṣatvādi janayan  
svasmin na rūpādi-sambandhādhīnaś cākṣuṣatvādau। 

**English**—
We see e.g. that colour, through its conjunction with earth and the like, produces in them the quality of visibility, but does not itself depend for its visibility on conjunction with colour. 

###### nigamanam
**vi॰pra॰**—
atō 'nubhūtir  
ātmanaḥ prakāśamānatvē,  
"+++(vastv-antaram)+++ prakāśata" iti vyavahārē ca  
svayam ēva hētuḥ॥

**English**—
Hence consciousness is itself the cause of its own 'shining forth,' as well as of the empirically observed shining forth of objects such as jars and the like.

###### nityatā
**English**—
Consciousness is eternal and incapable of change.

**vi॰pra॰**—
sēyaṁ svayaṁ-prakāśā'nubhūtir nityā ca,  
prāg-abhāvādy--a-bhāvāt। 

**English**—
This self-luminous consciousness, further, is eternal, for it is not capable of any form of non-existence – whether so – called antecedent non-existence or any other form. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
+++(prāg-abhāvādy→)+++tad-abhāvaś ca svatas-siddhatvād ēva। 

**English**—
This follows from its being self-established. 

###### na prāg-abhāvaḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
na hy anubhūtēs svatas-siddhāyāḥ prāg-abhāvas  
svatō 'nyatō vā'vagantuṁ śakyatē। 

**English**—
For the antecedent non-existence of self-established consciousness cannot be apprehended either through consciousness or anything else. 

###### nānubhūtēḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
anubhūtis svābhāvam avagamayantī satī  
tāvan nāvagamayati। +++(4)+++

**English**—
If consciousness itself gave rise to the apprehension of its own non-existence, it could not do so in so far as 'being,' for that would contradict its being; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
tasyās sattvē  
virōdhād ēva tad-abhāvō nāstīti  
kathaṁ sā svābhāvam avagamayati? 

**English**—
if it is, i.e. if its non-existence is not, how can it give rise to the idea of its non-existence? 

**vi॰pra॰**—
ēvam asaty api nāvagamayati;  
anubhūtis svayam a-satī  
svābhāvē kathaṁ pramāṇaṁ bhavēt? 

**English**—
Nor can it do so if not being; for if consciousness itself is not, how can it furnish a proof for its own non-existence? 

###### nānyataḥ
**vi॰pra॰**—
nāpy anyatō 'vagantuṁ śakyatē,  
anubhūtēr an-anya-gōcaratvāt। +++(4)+++

**English**—
Nor can the non- existence of consciousness be apprehended through anything else; for consciousness cannot be the object of anything else. 

**vi॰pra॰**—
asyāḥ prāg-abhāvaṁ sādhayat pramāṇam  
"anubhūtir iyam" iti viṣayī kr̥tya  
tad-abhāvaṁ sādhayēt;  

**English**—
Any instrument of knowledge proving the non-existence of consciousness, could do so only by making consciousness its object--'this is consciousness'; 

**vi॰pra॰**—
svatas-siddhatvēna "iyam" iti viṣayī-kārānarhātvāt,  
na tat-prāg-abhāvō 'nyataḥ śakyāvagamaḥ।

**English**—
but consciousness, as being self-established, does not admit of that objectivation which is implied in the word 'this,' and hence its previous non-existence cannot be proved by anything lying outside itself.

###### nōtpattiḥ

**vi॰pra॰**—
atō 'syāḥ prāg-abhāvābhāvād  
utpattir na śakyatē vaktum  
ity utpatti-pratisambaddhāś cānyē'pi bhāva-vikārās tasyā na santi॥

**English**—
As consciousness thus does not admit of antecedent non-existence, it further cannot be held to originate, and hence also all those other states of being which depend on origination cannot be predicated of it.

###### na nānā
###### anutpannatvāt
**vi॰pra॰**—
anutpannēyam anubhūtir  
ātmani nānātvam api na sahatē,  
vyāpaka-+++(anutpannatākhya-)+++viruddhōpalabdhēḥ ॥ 

**English**—
As consciousness is beginningless,  
it further does not admit of any plurality within itself;  
for we observe in this case  
the presence of something which is contrary to what invariably accompanies plurality  
(this something being 'beginninglessness' which is contrary to the quality of having a beginning--  
which quality invariably accompanies plurality). 

**vi॰pra॰**—
na hyanutpannaṁ nānābhūtaṁ dr̥ṣṭam। 

**English**—
